StatComp Project 2: Scottish weather

Yichao Wang (s2056237)

Seasonal variability

Is precipitation seasonally varying?

We aim to investigate the variability of Scottish perception and temperature data across a span of approximately sixty years by first loading the data \(\textbf{ghcnd_stations}\) and \(\textbf{ghcnd_values}\), and then combine them with the left_jiont function into a new data frame called ghcnd. To facilitate analysis, a single year was selected for examination, specifically the year 2008. We filter the data on Year == 2008 and create two plots to displaying the daily precipitation and temperature behaviors respectively.

Generally, we first focus on the analysis on precipitation data by filtering on Element == "PRCP". The result is shown on scatter plot where each dot represent the precipitation data for the specific day and there is a smooth line in darkblue shows the monthly average precipitation across the whole year. To be more specific, the plot shows the result for each station by applying facet_wrap function.

Here we set April to September as summer and other month to be winter. The trend on these plots indicate that several station have more volatility, for instance Ardtalnaig and Benmore: Younger Bontanic Garden, whereas the others are more smooth. To be more specifically, Ardtalnaig and Benmore: Younger Bontanic Garden station exhibit higher amounts of precipitation during winter months and lower amounts during summer months, whereas the opposite is true for the other stations, except for Braemar, where the precipitation is consistent throughout the year.

Similarly to the previous step for precipitation, we select the temperature data by filtering on Element %in% c("TMAX", "TMIN"). It is evident that there is a seasonal effect with the temperature being always higher in summer and lower in winter. this trend was observed in all stations which exactly coincide with the seasonal effect above.

To further analyze the precipitation, there is Monte Carlo permutation test for the hypotheses that we want to test: \[ \begin{align*} & H_0: \text{The rainfall distribution is the same in winter as in summer} \\ & H_1: \text{The winter and summer distributions have different expected values} \end{align*} \] We define the test statistics as the absoluate value of the difference between average precipitation in winter and summer for each station respectively as \(T = |\text{winter average} - \text{summer average}|\). For convinence, we add a \(\textbf{Summer}\) column to the data that is \(\textbf{TRUE}\) for summer month and \(\textbf{FALSE}\) for winter month by the mutate function. We first calculate the test statistics \(T\) for each station.

We do a randomized permutation test, since we have no model for the distribution of the data, by defining a function p_value_CI which calculate the p-value, Monte Carlo standard deviation and the confidence interval for p-value. Then, we count the number of times when the observed value(\(T_{obs}\)) is greater than or equal to the test statistic(\(T\)), \(T_{obs} \ge T\). Further, the Porject2Hint document provided the model for the count, \(X\), and the p-value as \[ X \sim \text{Bin}(N, p), \quad \text{and}\quad p = \mathbb{P}(T_{obs} \ge T | H_0). \] where \(N\) represents the number of permutations we take. Then we have \(\mathbb{E}(X) = Np\), and \(\text{Var}(X) = Np(1-p)\). To do the further evaluation about the value of \(p\), we can estimate it with \(\hat{p} = x/N\) and thus implied that the expected value and variance of \(\hat{p}\) are \[ \mathbb{E}(\hat{p}) = p, \quad \text{and}\quad \text{Var}(\hat{p}) = \frac{p(1-p)}{N}. \] Therefore, computing the p-values for each station and determining their Monte Carlo standard deviation can be accomplished by calculating \(x/N\) and taking the square root of their variance, which is given by \(\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{N}}\). Moreover, with sufficiently large values of \(N\), we can calculate the \(95\%\) confidence interval for the p-values by \[ \text{CI} = \hat{p}\pm z_{0.975}\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{N}} \] Despite that most of the observed values of count is zero, resulting in a p-value approaching zero due to a fixed \(N>0\), we can instead calculate a confidence interval for this case by the interval \([0, 1-0.0025^{1/N}]\). By applying the p_value_CI function, the resulting table shows the p-value, Monte Carlo standard deviation, and corresponding confidence interval for the p-value of each station.

Here we set \(N=10000\) and rejected the null hypothesis for each station where the corresponding p-value is less than 0.05. The table shows that most stations have a p-value of zero, but EDINBURGH: ROYAL BOTANIC GARDE and LEUCHARS have positive p-values. Notably, the p-value for EDINBURGH: ROYAL BOTANIC GARDE is surprisingly large, which indicates that we failed to reject the null hypothesis of no seasonal difference in rainfall distribution. Conversely, for LEUCHARS, the p-value is positive but less than 0.05, allowing us to reject the null hypothesis. Therefore, except for EDINBURGH: ROYAL BOTANIC GARDE, we reject the null hypothesis for all stations, indicating that a seasonal difference in rainfall distribution exists at these seven stations.

Spatial weather prediction

Estimation and prediction

For the second part of the project, we begin by modifying our data frame with the code below. We calculate the square root of the monthly averaged precipitation value and store it as a new variable called \(\textbf{Value_sqrt_avg}\). This generates a new data frame \(\textbf{ghcnd_spatial}\).

# Construct a version of the data set with a new variable, Value_sqrt_avg
# Subset the data to include only precipitation values
ghcnd_prcp<- ghcnd %>%
  filter(Element == "PRCP")
# Group by name, year, and month and compute the average value
ghcnd_spatial <- ghcnd_prcp %>%
  group_by(ID, Year, Month) %>%
  summarise(DecYear = mean(DecYear), Value_monthly = mean(Value), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(Value_sqrt_avg = sqrt(Value_monthly))

Now there is a basic model for the square root of monthly average precipitation defined as \[ M_0: \text{Value_sqrt_avg} \sim \text{Intercept + Longtitude + Latitude + Elevation + DecYear} \] Then by adding covariates \(\cos{(2\pi kt)}\) and \(\sin{(2\pi kt)}\) of frequencey \(k=1,2,3\)… we can also model the seasonal variability, defining four models \(M_1\), \(M_2\), \(M_3\), and \(M_4\), where the predictor expression for model \(M_K\) adds \[ \sum_{k=1}^{K} [\gamma_{c,k} \cos{(2\pi kt)} + \gamma_{s,k} \sin{(2\pi kt)}] \] to the \(M_0\) predictor expression, for the model coefficient \(\gamma_{c,k}\) and \(\gamma_{s,k}\). Moreover, the time \(t\) here is defined to be the \(\textbf{DecYear}\).

Now we aim to estimate the model parameters for all five models. We defined the function fit_model which takes the value of the corresponding data frame and the value of k, which respond to each model, and return the result of the fitted model. Further, with the help of summary function, we finally obtain the estimation of parameters for all models.

For model \(M_0\) below, we found the estimate for longitude and latitude are both negative, which suggests that there is a slight decrease in precipitation as we move westwards and northwards. Moreover, the estimate for elevation and DecYear are both positive and very small, indicating that there is a slight increase in precipitation over the year with increasing elevation.

Assessment: Station and season differences

To do the further investigation, we are looking for how well the model can predict precipitation at new location by constructing a stratified corss-validation. Here we define the stratified_cv function which takes two parameters, data frame and the value of k, which define one of the five models. The function will return a 96*5 dataframe shows the average SE and DS scores for each month by station after the corss validation process, including the Name, ID, Month, and its corresponding standard error scores(SE) and Dawid-Sebastiani scores(DS). Since there are 8 stations and 12 months, each of the five models will have exactly one result with \(8 \times 12 = 96\) rows. Thus, there will be a total of \(96\times 5 = 480\) rows across all five models, which means a total of \(2 \times 480 = 960\) number of values of scores(480 for SE score and 480 for DS scores).

For example, when choose \(k=1\), the result will return a table with 96 rows.

stratified_cv(ghcnd_data, 1)

In the table, we can see that the value of the SE score and DS score for each station is quite similar across models \(M_1\), \(M_2\), \(M_3\), and \(M_4\), but for model \(M_0\) they are quiet different. To view the difference more intuitively, we can create two subplots, one for the SE score and one for the DS score, to find out whether the models are equally effective at predicting the different stations.

The plot shows the same result as the table above, indicating that the value of both the SE score and DS score for all stations in the other four models are pretty similar, with slightly little fluctuation in the lines. However, the values for the \(M_0\) model are quite different. These findings imply that compare to the other four models, the \(M_0\) model lacks accuracy in predicting the precipitation at new location.

To further investigate whether the prediction accuracy is consistent throughout the year, we generate two plots that display the monthly average values of the two scores for each station of five models.

We found that the trend in both scores for each station is quite similar, and there exists visible gaps in the values of the two scores for each station between model \(M_0\) and the other four models for each month. This suggests that the \(M_0\) model lacks accuracy in predicting precipitation at new locations across the whole year. Additionally, it is obvious that the EDINBURGH: ROYAL BOTANIC GARDEN station is difficult to model, as the trend in both scores is significantly different from the trend of all other stations. Hence, the chance of encountering error increases when we apply stratified cross-validation that groups the data by station.

# Yichao Wang (s2056237)

# You can also include any needed library() calls here
library(StatCompLab)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(knitr)
library(dplyr)

###################

#' P-value and confidence interval
#' Construct the 95% confidence interval for each station
#'
#' The result will return a table includes the Name, p-value, 
#' Monte Carlo standard deviation, and the CI for each station.
#'
#' @param data the desired data to be put into model
#' @param alpha the value of alpha, here we take 0.05 to construct a 95% CI
#' @param N the number of permutations
#' 

p_value_CI <- function(data, alpha=0.05, N=10000) {
  # Initialize the count to be zero for each test statistic
  count <- rep(0, length = length(T_stats))
  for (n in 1:N) {
    # Generate a random permutation of the indices
    permutation <- sample(data$Summer, length(data$Summer), replace = FALSE)
    # Apply the permutation to the data and group by weather station
    ghcnd_permutation <- data %>%
      mutate("Summer" = permutation) %>%
      group_by(Name)
    # Compute the test statistic for the permuted data
    ghcnd_permutated <- ghcnd_permutation %>%
      summarise(Value = abs(mean(Value[Summer]) - mean(Value[!Summer])), .groups = "drop")
    # add one to the count if the test statistic is less than or equal to the observed value
    count <- count + (ghcnd_permutated$Value >= T_stats)
  }
  
  # Compute the p-value and Monte Carlo standard deviation
  p_value <- count / N
  monte_carlo_sd <- sqrt(p_value * (1 - p_value) / N)
  
  # Compute confidence interval for p-value
  lower_CI <- numeric(length(p_value))
  upper_CI <- numeric(length(p_value))
  for (i in 1:length(p_value)) {
    if (p_value[i] > 0) { # When x > 0 (p_value>0)
      lower_CI[i] <- p_value[i] - qnorm(1 - alpha/2) * monte_carlo_sd[i]
      upper_CI[i] <- p_value[i] + qnorm(1 - alpha/2) * monte_carlo_sd[i]
    } else { # When x = 0, CI=(0, 1-0.0025^(1/N))
      lower_CI[i] <- 0
      upper_CI[i] <- 1 - 0.025^(1/N)
    }
  }
  
  # Store the result in a dataframe and show them as a table
  result_table <- data.frame(Name = unique(winter_avg$Name), 
                             p_value = p_value,
                             monte_carlo_sd = monte_carlo_sd,
                             lower_CI = lower_CI,
                             upper_CI = upper_CI)
  return(kable(result_table, align = "lcccc"))
}




#' Estimate models for the square root of the 
#' monthly averaged precipitation values in Scotland
#'
#' The result will return the fitted model for five different 
#' model M0, M1, M2, M3, M4 as different value of k entered
#'
#' @param data the desired data to be put into model
#' @param k the model M_k(k from 0 to 4)
#' 

fit_model <- function(data, k) {
  # Define the formula for the model
  if(k == 0) { # When k = 0 
    model <- Value_sqrt_avg ~ Longitude + Latitude + Elevation + DecYear
  } else{ # When k = 1,2,3,4
    model <- formula(paste0("Value_sqrt_avg ~ Longitude + Latitude + Elevation + DecYear + ",
                            paste0("cos(2*pi*", seq(1, k), "*DecYear) + sin(2*pi*", seq(1, k), "*DecYear)", 
                                   collapse = " + ")))
  }
  # Fit the linear model
  fit <- lm(model, data = data)
  
  # Return the model object
  return(fit)
}




#' Stratified cross validation function
#' 
#' The result will return a 96*5 dataframe shows the average SE and DS scores for each 
#' month by station after the corss validation process, including the Name, ID, Month,
#' and its corresponding standard error scores(SE) and Dawid-Sebastiani scores(DS). 
#'
#' since there are 8 stations and 12 months, we got a total of 12*8=96 rows.
#' 
#' @param data the desired data to do the corss validation
#' @param k the model M_k(k from 0 to 4)

stratified_cv <- function(data, k) {
  pred2 <- data %>% mutate(mean = NA_real_, sd = NA_real_)
  for (id in unique(data$ID)) {
    if(k == 0) { # When k = 0 
      model <- Value_sqrt_avg ~ Longitude + Latitude + Elevation + DecYear
    } else{ # When k = 1,2,3,4
      model <- formula(paste0("Value_sqrt_avg ~ Longitude + Latitude + Elevation + DecYear + ",
                              paste0("cos(2*pi*", seq(1, k), "*DecYear) + sin(2*pi*", seq(1, k), "*DecYear)", 
                                     collapse = " + ")))
    }
    # fit and predict the model for the data
    fit <- lm(model, data %>% filter(ID != id))
    pred <- predict(fit, newdata = data %>% filter(ID == id), se.fit = TRUE)
    # evaluate the mean and sd
    pred2$mean[(pred2$ID == id)] <- pred$fit
    pred2$sd[(pred2$ID == id)] <- sqrt((pred$se.fit)^2 + (pred$residual.scale)^2)
    # mutate the table
    pred2 <- pred2 %>%
      group_by(ID, Name, Year, Month) %>%
      mutate(se = proper_score("se", Value_sqrt_avg, mean = mean),
             ds = proper_score("ds", Value_sqrt_avg, mean = mean, sd = sd))
  }
  # Calculate the average score for each month
  Average_score <- pred2 %>%
    group_by(ID, Name, Month) %>%
    summarise(se = mean(se), ds = mean(ds), .groups = "drop")
  return(Average_score)
}
